analysis.one_liner: Sends families a fully refundable monthly child tax credit, up to $300 per child.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 211 House cosponsors, all Democrats, and was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on its introduction day, where no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace today's child tax credit with a larger, fully refundable one paid monthly: $250 a month for each child age 6 through 17, $300 a month for each child under 6, and a $2,000 payment for the first month of a newborn's life. The full credit would go to families below $150,000 (joint) or $112,500 (single) in income, phase down gradually above that, and disappear only above $400,000 (joint) or $200,000 (single). It also adds a $500 credit for other dependents and directs the Treasury to deliver the credit as monthly payments through an online enrollment portal, with the amounts rising each year with inflation. The bill text contains no tax increases or spending cuts to pay for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 18, most directly those with low and moderate incomes: the credit is fully refundable, so a family owing little or no income tax still receives the full monthly amount, and payments arrive monthly rather than as a once-a-year tax refund. Parents of newborns get an extra-large first-month payment, and families caring for non-child dependents get a $500 credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially low-income ones

how_it_helps.text: Creates a fully refundable child tax credit of $250 per month for each child age 6 or older and $300 per month (120% of $250) for each child under 6, with the first month of a newborn's life paid at 800% of the $250 rate ($2,000), so the credit goes to families regardless of how much tax they owe.

Replaces the annual-credit structure with a Treasury-run program of monthly advance payments, including a presumptive-eligibility system, automatic enrollment after a birth, an online portal available in multiple languages, and grace periods of 3 to 6 months when a family misses a renewal.

The credit phases down with income but never below the equivalent of $2,000 per child per year until household income exceeds $400,000 (joint) or $200,000 (single), and amounts are indexed to inflation starting in 2024.
Adds a $500 credit for certain other dependents, such as elderly or disabled relatives cared for by the taxpayer.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers, because the bill text contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts; the credit is deficit-financed. High-income households give up part of the credit through the income phase-downs, and a permanent expansion on this scale would increase federal deficits substantially.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue provisions at all — it creates the credit without any tax increase or spending cut to offset it — so a permanent expansion of roughly this scale would add on the order of $100 billion a year to federal deficits.

Today's child tax credit is worth the most to families that owe income tax, and its refundable portion is tied to earnings; the new fully refundable credit decouples the money from work, an objection its critics have consistently raised and an honest supporter must weigh against the poverty reduction.
Monthly advance payments create recapture risk: a family whose income rises sharply mid-year or whose filing status changes can owe back some of the money it already received.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and direct: cash to nearly every family with children, with the biggest gains for families the current credit reaches least. The cost is real and the bill does not address it — no offsets, a permanent open-ended entitlement indexed to inflation. It was also written as a single-party bill with no Republican cosponsors, which both reflected and guaranteed its fate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, without a hearing, markup, or floor vote, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 7, 2023, and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Its only two actions in the entire 118th Congress are the introduction and that committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred.
It accumulated 211 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, including the House Democratic leadership, but no Republicans.
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, without the committee ever taking up the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No family gained the monthly payments, because the bill never moved. The federal Treasury was spared the added deficit spending, and families that owe substantial income tax kept the existing credit structure, which pays them more per child than it pays low-income families. The Ways and Means majority also kept a single-party tax bill off the committee agenda without having to vote against it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury spared spending; the agenda-holder

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Family Act and recruited 210 cosponsors, continuing her years-long push to make the expanded 2021 child tax credit permanent.

for.name: Suzan DelBene and Ritchie Torres
for.role: Co-lead original cosponsors, U.S. Representatives (D-WA, D-NY)
for.what_they_did: Joined as the first-named cosponsors on the introduction.

for.name: House Democratic leadership and caucus
for.role: 211 cosponsors, including Hakeem Jeffries, Nancy Pelosi, and Steny Hoyer
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including the party's top three House leaders, but the bill never received committee or floor action during their minority.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote during the two and a half years it sat in his committee.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controlled the House floor and committee agendas in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Allowed no consideration of the bill; no Republican cosponsored it and no floor vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 211 cosponsors were Democrats and none was a Republican, and the bill was referred to a committee chaired by a Republican who took no action on it.

industries.note: The credit would phase down above $150,000 (joint) and disappear above $400,000 (joint), so wealthy families would lose the largest credits they can currently claim per child. Their broader interest in lower deficits, however, argues the other way, since the bill is deficit-financed.

The bill creates a large permanent, inflation-indexed entitlement with no offsets in the bill text; the cost falls on the Treasury and, over time, on taxpayers generally. This is the standard trade-off of any large social spending bill, not a transfer to a private industry.
